cards.front: What is a direct object pronoun?
cards.back:
A direct object pronoun replaces the noun that directly receives the action of a verb (no preposition between verb and noun):
  I see the woman → I see her. (her = direct object pronoun)
  Veo a la mujer → La veo.
cards.grammarNote: In Spanish, direct object pronouns go BEFORE the conjugated verb in most cases.

cards.back:
me — me
te — you (tú)
lo — him / it (m.) / you (usted, m.)
la — her / it (f.) / you (usted, f.)
nos — us
os — you all (vosotros)
los — them (m.) / you all (ustedes, m.)
las — them (f.) / you all (ustedes, f.)
cards.grammarNote: Lo/la and los/las must agree in gender and number with the noun they replace.
Te replaces 'you' (tú) as the direct object. Te goes before the conjugated verb veo.

cards.front: I know her / I met her.
cards.grammarNote: La replaces her (feminine). Conocer (to know/meet a person) takes a direct object. La goes before conozco.

cards.front: I love him / I want it.
cards.grammarNote: Lo replaces him (m.) or a masculine noun (it). Querer + direct object = to love someone or to want something.
Te (you) is the direct object of llamar (to call). In Spanish, the present tense is often used to express a near-future promise: te llamo (I'll call you).

cards.front: I see her across the dance floor.
cards.back: La veo al otro lado de la pista de baile.
cards.grammarNote: La replaces the woman (fem. noun). Al otro lado de = on the other side of.

cards.front: The bartender is treating us (to a drink).
cards.grammarNote: Nos (us) is the direct object of invitar. Here nos goes before the conjugated verb nos invita.

cards.front: Where does the pronoun go with an infinitive?
cards.back:
Option 1 — before the conjugated verb:
  Te quiero ver esta noche. (I want to see you tonight.)
Option 2 — attached to the infinitive:
  Quiero verte esta noche.
cards.grammarNote: Both placements are equally correct. Attaching to the infinitive requires no written accent unless the word becomes 4+ syllables.
With progressive (estar + gerund), the pronoun can go before estar or attach to the gerund. When attaching, an accent is added to preserve stress: buscándote.
In affirmative commands, the pronoun attaches to the end. An accent is added: llama + me → llámame (to preserve original stress on lla-).

cards.front: Don't call me late. (negative command + pronoun)
cards.grammarNote: In negative commands, the pronoun goes BEFORE the verb. Me stays separate: no me llames.

cards.front: Lo vs. Le — which is correct for 'I see him'?
cards.back:
Standard Spanish: Lo veo. (I see him.)
In Spain: Le veo. (leísmo — le used for masculine people as direct object)
Both are widely accepted, but lo veo is the standard taught in Latin America.
cards.grammarNote: Leísmo (using le instead of lo for masculine people) is common in Spain and considered correct there, but lo is the international standard.

cards.front: What happens when you have both a direct AND indirect object pronoun?
cards.back:
Both appear before the verb, with the indirect object pronoun first:
  Me lo da. (She gives it to me.) — me = indirect, lo = direct
If the indirect is le/les, it changes to se before lo/la:
  Se lo doy. (I give it to her/him.)
cards.grammarNote: Remember: indirect before direct (ID). And le/les → se when followed by lo/la/los/las.

cards.front: Replace the nouns: I want to see the woman again. The DJ is playing that song. Call me tomorrow.
cards.back:
Quiero verla de nuevo. / La quiero ver de nuevo.
El DJ lo está poniendo. / El DJ está poniéndolo.
¡Llámame mañana!
cards.grammarNote: La (her, fem.) for the woman. Lo (it, masc.) for the song (la canción is fem. — so la: el DJ la está poniendo). Llámame attaches the pronoun to the affirmative command.
